newsitem.title: MEXICO: Robust Mexico peso product of circumstance -Werner.
newsitem.headline: Robust Mexico peso product of circumstance -Werner.

text.p: Mexico's peso has defied expectations of a depreciation because of domestic economic strength and liquidity conditions abroad, Deputy Finance Minister Martin Werner said on Tuesday.

In an interview with Reuters he said foreign and local circumstances had kept inflows higher than foreseen, holding the peso within an unusually narrow trading band for most of this year -- despite economists' projections.
"There are two very clear factors: the evolution of the Mexican economy has continued better than expected, which has brought more inflows to Mexico," Werner said.

"The liquidity conditions in the international markets have also been better than expected -- this has produced more inflows into Mexico and has meant that the exchange rate has slightly appreciated."
But he would not be drawn on why no "stepwise adjustment" -- brusque fall -- had occurred in the way market analysts had forecast.
Some were predicting the peso would ease around the time of mid-term elections on July 6. However this failed to materialise and some now estimate the currency is around 10 percent overvalued.
Some economists also warn the longer the peso takes to adjust, the harder the fall when it comes.
The currency closed on Tuesday at 7.75 pesos to the dollar and this year has scarcely scraped the sides of a narrow 7.78 to 8.03 trading range.
Asked what the authorities could do if they were concerned the peso was trading too strongly, he said:

"Already the exchange commission has increased the level of the (dollar put) options to take advantage of circumstances to increase international reserves and also in a way to try to diminish some of the short-term pressures on the exchange rate."

In an unusual move at the end of July Mexico's exchange commission -- made up of central bank and Finance Ministry members with a Finance Ministry majority -- signalled it would like to see a weaker peso by increasing the amount of dollar put options it planned to auction in August.
But the move, accompanied by a statement of concern about the effect the peso strength would have on the economy, did little to dent the exchange rate.
Werner said this was largely due to those same internal and external pressures.
"What happened was the international conjuncture was very favourable and Mexico's economy is going along well," he said.
But he added: "As seen in the exchange commision's press release there are certain concerns because large short-term flows can move the exchange rate beyond what equilibrium would indicate."
Mexico is widely expected to move into a trade deficit in the second half of the year, and some economists say this may impact on the currency markets.

"The economy has been strong and this has produced an exchange rate slightly stronger than we expected, but eventually if there were a bigger than expected deterioration in the external accounts, that at some moment would lead to an adjustment in the exchange rate," Werner said in the interview.
However he insisted that the economy was far less vulnerable to external shocks than it has been in the past.
"We have confidence that the market will adjust the exchange rate to give an exchange rate of equilibrium," he added. ((--Mexico City newsroom +525 728 7905))
